name: Milestone 16: Benchmarks
description:
Triage: ready-for-agent

## Problem Statement

We do not know how fast rocco is. No document states a frame budget, a capacity or the cost of the seam. The docs claim the renderer "never allocates per frame up to 4096 draws", but nobody measured it. The design has a cost that critics will question: a pure game behind a seam, with a Scene rebuilt every fixed step. We want numbers that a skeptical reader accepts, and we want enough of them to write a blog post about what the engine can do.

Today, measurement is not fair:

- Every build, `--release` included, passes `-debug`. The host then wraps its allocator in a tracking allocator.
- The Roc heap uses a tracking allocator with a hash map. `roc_realloc` always allocates a new block and copies.
- Fixed steps follow the wall clock, so a slow Frame runs more fixed steps on the next Frame. The work changes with the measurement.
- Every run opens a window, so the GPU driver and the compositor add noise to CPU numbers.
- The examples are small and stress nothing.
- Only `step` and `view` are timed, and only when `ROCCO_ALLOC_REPORT=1`.

## Solution

Build a benchmark harness that measures CPU time per Span inside the engine, on true release builds, with a fixed workload per run.

- The main question is the cost of the seam. The second question is capacity: how far each axis scales before a Frame misses its budget.
- Bench games each scale one axis: Draws, Colliders, Model size and UI. A mixed bench game scales all axes together and gives the headline figure.
- Odin twins of the Model size and Colliders bench games run the same logic with no Roc. The difference is the cost of the seam.
- Lockstep and Headless run modes make each run do the same work.
- A fixed statistical protocol, a committed summary per run and a method document let a reader check every claim.
- The Roc heap gets an A/B comparison: the current allocation map against a size header, in the same commit.

The headline figure is: the largest N for which p99 Frame CPU time stays under 16.6 ms, at 2 fixed steps per Frame, on the reference machine.

## User Stories

1. As the engine author, I want `--release` to build without `-debug`, so that release numbers describe the engine that ships.
2. As the engine author, I want the host tracking allocator only when a build asks for it, so that shipped builds do not pay for it.
3. As the engine author, I want `alloc-check.sh` to ask for the tracking allocator explicitly, so that the allocation checks keep working.
4. As a game author, I want the words after my game's name on the command line in Config as Args, so that my game can take arguments.
5. As a game author, I want the host to pass Args unparsed, so that their meaning is my game's decision.
6. As a bench game, I want to read N from Args, so that one binary runs at every size.
7. As the engine author, I want a Lockstep mode set by `ROCCO_LOCKSTEP=1`, so that each Frame runs exactly one fixed step and one render.
8. As the engine author, I want vsync off in Lockstep, so that frame pacing does not hide CPU time.
9. As the engine author, I want a Headless mode set by `ROCCO_HEADLESS=1`, so that seam and simulation runs have no window, no GPU and no compositor noise.
10. As the engine author, I want Headless to always run in Lockstep, so that a Headless run has a fixed workload.
11. As the engine author, I want Lockstep and Headless in the shipped binary, so that the benchmark runs the exact binary that ships.
12. As the engine author, I want a Headless run to answer Queries, so that the Colliders axis measures real query work.
13. As the engine author, I want an invalid value of a new environment variable rejected at startup, so that a typo cannot produce a silent normal run.
14. As the engine author, I want a Span for the input copy, so that I see the cost of copying Input into Roc.
15. As the engine author, I want a Span for `step`, so that I see the game's simulation cost.
16. As the engine author, I want a Span for Command execution and decref, so that I see the cost of Commands.
17. As the engine author, I want a Span for `view`, so that I see the cost of building the Scene.
18. As the engine author, I want a Span for collision and Queries, so that I see the engine's physics cost.
19. As the engine author, I want a Span for the QueryResults copy, so that I see the cost of returning answers to Roc.
20. As the engine author, I want a Span for Scene interpolation, so that I see the cost of the Pairing.
21. As the engine author, I want a Span for UI layout, so that I see the cost of Clay.
22. As the engine author, I want a Span for render submit, so that I see the cost of one draw call per Draw.
23. As the engine author, I want a Span for `sg.commit`, so that I see the cost of the final submit.
24. As the engine author, I want Spans compiled out unless a build asks for them, so that shipped builds pay nothing.
25. As the engine author, I want the timer overhead measured once and reported, so that a reader knows the error in each Span.
26. As the engine author, I want one CSV row per Frame, so that I can compute percentiles over Frames.
27. As the engine author, I want a Draws bench game with N moving primitive cubes, one Light and shadows on, so that I measure render submit and the Pairing.
28. As the engine author, I want a Colliders bench game with N moving Colliders and a fixed set of 8 raycasts, 8 overlaps and one ContactsOf query, so that I measure the broadphase and the queries.
29. As the engine author, I want a Model size bench game with N entities and a fixed 100 Draws, so that I measure Roc's cost with the render cost fixed.
30. As the engine author, I want an idiomatic and a tuned version of the Model size bench game, so that I can report the cost of ordinary Roc code compared with code that keeps the Model unique.
31. As the engine author, I want a UI bench game with N Box and Text elements, so that I measure Clay layout.
32. As the engine author, I want each bench game to change only one axis, so that a curve shows one cause.
33. As the engine author, I want N in powers of two from 64 to 16,384, so that the curves show scaling and the step above 4,096 Draws.
34. As the engine author, I want a mixed bench game whose one N scales Draws, Colliders and UI together at a stated ratio, so that I have one realistic headline figure.
35. As the engine author, I want an Odin twin of the Model size bench game, so that I isolate the cost of the seam for simulation.
36. As the engine author, I want an Odin twin of the Colliders bench game, so that I isolate the cost of the seam for queries.
37. As the engine author, I want each Odin twin to use the same logic and Model layout as its bench game, so that the comparison is fair.
38. As the engine author, I want the Odin twins to run through the same run loop as Roc games, so that only the game differs.
39. As the engine author, I want a run with an empty `step`, so that I know the lower limit of the seam.
40. As the engine author, I want the Roc heap to use either the allocation map or a size header, chosen at compile time, so that I can compare both from one commit.
41. As the engine author, I want both Roc heap versions to pass one test suite, so that the comparison is between two correct allocators.
42. As the engine author, I want the size header to grow a block in place when the backing allocator can, so that realloc avoids the copy.
43. As the engine author, I want the losing Roc heap version deleted after the comparison, so that the switch does not stay.
44. As the engine author, I want the summary to report realloc counts, so that the A/B result has a cause.
45. As the engine author, I want a `bench` subcommand in `scripts/build.roc`, so that one command builds and runs a sweep.
46. As the engine author, I want each configuration to run 120 warmup Frames and 2,000 measured Frames, so that the numbers come from steady state.
47. As the engine author, I want each configuration repeated in 5 processes, so that I see the spread between processes.
48. As the engine author, I want the configurations run in shuffled order, so that thermal drift spreads across all configurations.
49. As the engine author, I want the median, p95, p99 and max of each Span, so that the mean does not hide stutters.
50. As the engine author, I want each summary to record the machine, the OS, the power state, the git hash and the build flags, so that a reader can repeat the run.
51. As the engine author, I want the analysis script to refuse a summary from a debug build, so that a debug number cannot reach a chart.
52. As the engine author, I want summary JSON committed in a directory per date and machine, so that the blog can cite one result directory.
53. As the engine author, I want raw CSVs kept out of git, so that the repo stays small.
54. As the engine author, I want a Python script that draws the charts from summary JSON, so that anyone can redraw them.
55. As the engine author, I want one real-clock run of an existing example, so that I have a reference for what a player experiences.
56. As a blog reader, I want a method document, so that I can check how the numbers were made.
57. As a blog reader, I want the method to state that no cross-engine comparison was made and why, so that I know what the numbers do not claim.
58. As a CI maintainer, I want each bench game run once Headless in CI with no timing claims, so that the bench games do not rot.
59. As the engine author, I want the bench games out of `examples/`, so that `run-games.sh`, `test-all.sh` and `screenshot.sh` do not run them.
60. As the engine author, I want the harness to run on Windows with the same protocol, so that I can add Windows numbers later.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Glossary.** The spec uses the terms Lockstep, Headless, Bench game, Odin twin, Span and Args from `CONTEXT.md`.
- **Release build.** `--release` drops `-debug` and keeps `-o:speed`. The host tracking allocator is behind a compile-time define. `alloc-check.sh` and the dev builds set that define. Games keep Roc's default `--opt=speed`.
- **Args.** Config gets `args : List Str`: the words after the game's name, in the order typed. The host does not parse them. This is a Vocabulary change and rebuilds the host and every game. ADR 0006 records it and moves from "proposed" to "accepted" when this lands. The glue spec and the platform Config change together.
- **Run loop.** The lockstep loop becomes one procedure. It takes Game calls, the Args, a Frame count and a Span sink, and returns. Headless calls it directly. The windowed Lockstep mode drives the same per-Frame work from the sokol frame callback. The normal real-clock mode keeps its accumulator.
- **Run modes.** `ROCCO_LOCKSTEP=1` and `ROCCO_HEADLESS=1` are parsed by pure functions, in the same way as `ROCCO_EXIT_AFTER_FRAMES`. Headless implies Lockstep. Lockstep sets the swap interval so that vsync is off. Headless needs `ROCCO_EXIT_AFTER_FRAMES` or a Frame count, so it cannot run forever.
- **Headless and assets.** Headless skips the GPU work of a Load. It still runs `loaded` with the Manifest, so the game sees the same ids.
- **Spans.** A Span is a pair of `tick_now` reads around one named section. A compile-time define turns Spans on. Without it, the Span calls compile to nothing. The existing `step_us` and `view_us` in the alloc report line stay as they are, because `alloc-check.sh` parses that line.
- **Span sink.** The sink writes one CSV row per Frame: the Frame number, the fixed steps in the Frame, then one column per Span in microseconds. The first row is a header.
- **Roc heap.** A compile-time define, `ROCCO_ROC_HEAP`, chooses `map` or `header`. The header version stores the size in a header before each block. The header is at least 16 bytes and at least the alignment. Realloc reads the old size from the header and calls the backing allocator's resize. The `live` counter becomes `allocs - deallocs` in both versions. The leak report at shutdown exists only in the map version. After the comparison, one version is deleted, and so is the define.
- **Bench games.** They live in a top-level `bench/` directory with the Odin twins and the analysis tools. Each bench game reads N from the first Arg. Each bench game uses the Seed for its randomness, so a run is repeatable.
- **Odin twins.** Each twin implements Game calls in Odin. It keeps its Model in Odin structs with the same fields as the Roc Model and returns a Scene in the same Vocabulary types. A twin build links the twin instead of a Roc app.
- **Mixed bench game.** Each entity has one Draw and one Collider. Every 10 entities add one UI element. The Queries are fixed at 8 raycasts, 8 overlaps and one ContactsOf query. There are 4 Lights. The method document states this ratio.
- **Protocol.** For each configuration (one bench game, one N):
  1. Run 120 warmup Frames and drop them.
  2. Measure 2,000 Frames.
  3. Repeat in 5 separate processes.
  4. Shuffle the order of all configurations in a sweep.
- **Summary JSON.** One file per configuration with: the bench game, N, the run mode, per-Span median, p95, p99 and max, the spread between processes, the Roc heap counters, the git hash, the build flags, the `ODIN_DEBUG` state, the Roc heap version, the machine, the OS and the power state.
- **Results.** Summaries go in `bench/results/<date>-<machine>/`. Raw CSVs go in an ignored directory.
- **Analysis.** A Python script reads the summaries, refuses any summary from a debug build and draws one curve per axis, plus the twin comparisons and the Roc heap A/B.
- **Headline budget.** p99 Frame CPU time under 16.6 ms at 2 fixed steps per Frame. A Frame in Lockstep runs one fixed step, so the analysis computes the budget from the per-step Spans times 2 plus the per-Frame Spans. The method document states this calculation.
- **Method document.** `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` holds the protocol, the Spans, the build flags, the hardware rules, the headline definition, the reasons for no cross-engine comparison and a link to the latest results.
- **Hardware.** The reference machine is the author's Mac. Each run records the chip, the RAM, the OS, AC power and a cooldown between runs. Windows runs come later with the same protocol.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test checks behaviour that a caller sees, not internal steps. Tests call the public procedure or hook and check its result.
- **Run loop.** Tests drive the lockstep run loop with the existing fake game from the seam tests. They check:
  - N Frames give N `step` calls and N `view` calls.
  - Headless never calls sokol.
  - The Args reach `init` through Config, in order.
  - Every Frame gets every Span, in order.
  - A build without Spans records nothing.
  - Queries get answers in Headless.
- **Roc heap.** One test suite calls `roc_alloc`, `roc_dealloc` and `roc_realloc` directly. Both versions must pass it. It checks that realloc keeps the contents when a block grows and when it shrinks, that alignment holds, and that the counters agree. `alloc-check.sh` stays the end-to-end check.
- **Environment variables.** Parse tests for `ROCCO_LOCKSTEP` and `ROCCO_HEADLESS` follow the exit-after-frames tests.
- **Analysis script.** Unit tests on a small CSV fixture follow the release script tests. They check the warmup cut, the percentiles, the spread between processes, the refusal of a debug build and the shape of the summary JSON.
- **Bench games.** `roc test` covers their Stages, in the same way as the examples. CI runs each bench game once Headless as a smoke test.
- **Release flags.** No test checks the compiler flags directly. The summary records the build flags and the `ODIN_DEBUG` state, and the analysis script refuses a debug build.

## Out of Scope

- Regression tracking across commits. It gets a separate task.
- Comparisons with other engines.
- GPU timing.
- Timing claims from CI runners.
- Windows numbers in the first results. The harness must work there, but the first published run is on the Mac.
- Instancing, a broadphase for raycasts and overlaps, and other optimisations. The benchmarks may show that they are needed, but this spec only measures.
- The allocation pool behind `roc_alloc` and `roc_dealloc`. That task stays separate. It can join the Roc heap comparison later as a third version.
- A Light count axis. Lights are capped at 8.

## Further Notes

- The step in the Draws curve above 4,096 is expected, because the Pairing map is reserved for 4,096 Draws. Report it as a finding.
- The open task "The allocation pool behind roc_alloc and roc_dealloc" asks to measure before and after. This harness gives it that measurement.
- The open task "Debug and speed parity for allocator counters" depends on `alloc-check.sh`. After this spec, `alloc-check.sh` must set the tracking define explicitly.
- The blog post quotes `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` and cites one committed result directory.

name: The window options, the GPU sizes and the Launch check
description:
Triage: ready-for-agent

## Parent

Milestone 17: Launch (nm2ai3l5). Read it with `dex show nm2ai3l5 --full`. ADR 0007 and the CONTEXT.md entries for `launch` and Launch bind the design.

## What to build

The host reads the Launch's window and `shadow_map`, and checks the Launch.
One pure function takes a Launch and a run mode and returns the sokol
description: width, height, title, the sample count from the Msaa tag with
`Off` as one, `high_dpi`, `fullscreen` and vsync. Lockstep turns vsync off
whatever the Launch says. It replaces today's function of the run mode
alone. The mesh and UI pipelines take the sample count from the Launch, so
the swapchain and the pipelines match. The shadow map image takes
`shadow_map` on both sides. The Headless platform record takes the Launch's
width and height at dpi 1 and ignores the rest of the window. A pure Launch
check returns the name of the first bad field, or none: a zero width,
height or shadow map. The host prints the field with the rule it broke and
exits with status 1, as a bad `ROCCO_SEED` does. Each Launch field's doc
comment in the Vocabulary says whether a Scene field may replace it later
(`fullscreen`, `title`) and whether a run mode overrides it (vsync under
Lockstep, the whole window under Headless).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tests build the description from a Launch in each run mode and check
every field, the Msaa mapping, and vsync off only in Lockstep.
- [ ] Table tests over the Launch check: each zero field names itself, and
the default passes.
- [ ] A Headless frame test checks the UI window equals the Launch's width
and height at dpi 1.
- [ ] Manual check with `scripts/screenshot.sh` on a Retina Mac: the default
Launch gives a 1920 by 1080 PNG with the HUD at the same logical size as
before, and a game with a 1280 by 720 Launch opens at that size.
- [ ] The constants `SAMPLE_COUNT` and `SHADOW_MAP_SIZE` and the 960 by 540
literals leave the engine, except as the default's values in the Launch
module and the Headless fallback they replace.
- [ ] `scripts/test-all.sh` and `scripts/host-check.sh` pass.

## Blocked by

- 7jogcsso
result:
Read the window, the sample count and the shadow map from Launch. Engine change in 81adc13, screenshot tool in 24ab47c.

- app_desc(launch, mode, allocator) in engine/app.odin builds the sokol description from the Launch: width, height, title (a cstring from the allocator; sokol copies it at start), high_dpi, fullscreen, the sample count from the Msaa tag with Off as one, and vsync. Lockstep turns vsync off whatever the Launch says; the real clock follows the Launch. msaa_sample_count lives in engine/launch.odin.
- renderer_init takes the Launch: the mesh, sky and UI pipelines take the sample count from it and shadow_map_make takes shadow_map. SAMPLE_COUNT and SHADOW_MAP_SIZE are gone.
- headless_window and headless_platform in engine/frame.odin take the Launch's width and height at dpi 1. HEADLESS_WINDOW and HEADLESS_PLATFORM are gone. The only 960 by 540 left outside tests is launch_default.
- launch_check returns the name of the first zero field (window.width, window.height, shadow_map) or ok. Deviation: it returns the field name only, as the ticket says; the host prints the one rule. launch_check_or_exit runs between seam_launch and seam_init and exits with 1.
- The Vocabulary comments on Launch and Window say which field a later Scene field may replace (title, fullscreen) and which a run mode overrides (vsync under Lockstep, the window under Headless); a field with neither changes only on restart.

name: The full benchmark protocol
description:
Triage: ready-for-agent

## Parent

Milestone 16: Benchmarks (zbygy2an). Read it with `dex show zbygy2an --full`.

## What to build

The `bench` subcommand runs a sweep:

1. Run 120 warmup Frames and drop them.
2. Measure 2,000 Frames.
3. Repeat in 5 separate processes.
4. Shuffle the order of all configurations.

The summary adds the spread between processes, the Roc heap counters, the Roc heap version, the machine, the OS and the power state. Summaries go in `bench/results/<date>-<machine>/`. Raw CSVs go in a directory that git ignores. The Python script draws one curve per axis from the summaries.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One command runs a sweep over N from 64 to 16,384 in powers of two for one bench game.
- [ ] The summary drops the warmup Frames and reports the spread between the 5 processes.
- [ ] The summary records the machine, the OS, the power state, the git hash and the build flags.
- [ ] Python unit tests check the warmup cut, the spread and the summary shape.
- [ ] The chart script draws the Model size curve from committed summaries.
- [ ] The sweep runs on macOS and needs nothing that blocks Windows later.

## Blocked by

- h0w634tt
result: bench <game> [n] runs the shuffled 5-process protocol for Roc games and Odin twins and writes summaries to bench/results/

commit.message: merge: The full benchmark protocol (zi6urdhv)

name: Milestone 24: Animation
description:
Triage: ready-for-agent

## Problem Statement

The engine draws only rigid meshes. The glTF loader reads no Skin and no
Clip, and a Draw cannot name one. The tutorial character cannot walk, and
the "ready to announce" arc needs animated characters.

## Solution

The loader reads one Skin and its Clips per .glb. A Draw gains a Pose. The
host samples two Clips, mixes them by a fade, and skins the mesh on the
GPU. The tutorial Blender script rigs Pip, and chapter 10 walks Pip.

Done when Pip plays Idle while still and Walk while moving in tutorial
chapter 10, and fades between the two Clips.

Check:
- A Bridge screenshot, with a step that holds a key, shows Pip mid-walk.
- Odin tests cover the Clip sampler, the fade and the loader errors.
- Chapter 10 is in run-games, the alloc check, the Linux container list and
  CI.

## Decisions (grilled 2026-10-26)

- Vocabulary (one change):
  - A Draw gains `pose : { clip : U32, time : F32, fade_clip : U32,
    fade_time : F32, fade : F32 }`. `pf.Draw.default` gives all zeros.
  - Clip id 0 is no Clip: the mesh draws in its bind pose. Ids start at 1
    and are unique across a Pack.
  - Each Manifest mesh entry gains `clips : List({ name : Str, id : U32,
    duration : F32 })`.
  - A Draw that names a Clip of another mesh draws the bind pose. The host
    logs once.
- The Model owns the time and the fade. The game wraps a looping time with
  the duration. The host has no Loop or Once mode.
- The fade is in the one Vocabulary change, so a later fade needs no second
  change. The Model moves the weight; the host samples both Clips and mixes
  each Joint, with slerp for rotations.
- Clips are in place. No root motion.
- Loader: one Skin per .glb, at most 64 Joints. All primitives of the Skin
  merge in bind-pose space. More than one Skin, mixed skinned and unskinned
  mesh nodes, more than 64 Joints, and CUBICSPLINE keys each fail the load
  with an error. Files with no Skin load as today.
- Channels: translation, rotation and scale, LINEAR and STEP. No morph
  targets. No Clips on nodes with no Skin.
- `Skinned_Vertex`: the 48-byte Vertex plus `joints : [4]u8` and
  `weights : [4]u8` (normalised), 56 bytes. Own pipeline and own shadow
  pipeline.
- A skin uniform block per skinned Draw holds up to 64 Joint matrices
  (4 KB). The 256-byte cap stays for the other blocks.
- Normals use the skin matrix. A Joint must have no non-uniform scale; the
  guide says so.
- The box of a skinned mesh is padded at load by 25% of its largest extent,
  for culling and the shadow box.
- Between two Scenes, the renderer blends the time and the fade when the
  Clip is the same in both. Otherwise it takes the current values.
- No Joint read-back to the game.
- Words (CONTEXT.md): Clip (avoid "animation"), Clip id, Skin, Joint (avoid
  "bone"), Pose. The Draw field is `pose`.
- Roc helpers: `Mesh.clip(manifest, mesh, clip) -> U32` and
  `Mesh.clip_duration` in `packages/mesh/Mesh.roc`. A platform module
  `Pose` with `Pose.loop(time, duration)` and `Pose.still(clip, time)`.
- Rig: `examples/tutorial/source/make_meshes.py` builds about 12 Joints
  (root, hips, spine, head, upper and lower arm and leg each side), binds
  each limb island rigidly to one Joint, and keys Idle (about 2 s, breath
  bob) and Walk (1 s cycle) at 24 fps.
- Chapter 10 copies chapter 9. The Model advances the walk time by
  dt x speed / walk_speed and fades between Idle and Walk over 0.2 s. Guide
  page `guide/tutorial/10-animation.md` with region blocks.
- ADR 0016 is a draft now. The last task accepts it.

Code pointers:
`engine/gltf.odin` (merges every primitive and bakes world space at 417),
`engine/render.odin:7-11` (256-byte uniform cap) and 125-144 (shadow
pipeline), `engine/frame_render.odin` 297-320 (shadow box) and 538-546
(interpolation), `platform/Vocabulary.roc:105,154`, `engine/pack.odin:127-148`,
`engine/seam.odin:183-200`.
result: Pip plays Idle while still and Walk while moving in tutorial chapter 10, and fades between the two Clips over 0.2 s. The Bridge check holds D and checks the walk screenshot against a still one. The person played chapter 10 on macOS and walking works. CI passes on macOS, Linux and Windows (run 40283435567). All six subtasks are complete. PR #14.

name: Vec3 package: packages/linalg and the entity game uses it
description:
Triage: ready-for-agent

Move the Vec3 maths the entity game copies into a package. See the
decisions in Milestone 10 (72omk38x). Grilled 2026-10-13.

The package was first named packages/vec3. It was renamed to
packages/linalg on 2026-10-13 (eebe0aa), so Quat can join it and import Vec3.

## Requirements

1. Create packages/linalg/main.roc with header `package [Vec3] {}` and
packages/linalg/Vec3.roc as a type module, the same layout as packages/camera.
2. Vec3.roc declares its own structural `Vec3 : { x : F32, y : F32, z : F32 }`.
Inside the type module, annotations name it `Vec3.Vec3`. No package depends
on another package.
3. Expose zero, one, add, sub, neg, scale, dot, cross, length, normalize and
lerp. `lerp : Vec3, Vec3, F32 -> Vec3`. `normalize` of zero returns zero.
4. Give every function one expect with a known answer.
5. In examples/entity-game/main.roc, add `linalg: "../../packages/linalg/main.roc"`
to the header, import `linalg.Vec3 as V`, and delete the local origin, one,
add, scale and dot. Keep rotate_y and pi; the quaternion ticket removes
rotate_y.
6. Run `roc test examples/entity-game/main.roc` and `roc test
packages/linalg/main.roc`.

## Not in scope

- No change to platform/Vocabulary.roc. The vocabulary keeps its own Vec3.
- No change to packages/camera or packages/mesh.
- No rotate or quaternion function.

## Done when

- Both test runs pass.
- `roc scripts/build.roc -- game entity-game` builds and the game runs as
before on arm64mac.
- scripts/alloc-check.sh still reports 3 for entity-game.
result: Added the Vec3 package as packages/vec3 (2ed75a3) and moved the entity game onto it. Renamed it to packages/linalg in eebe0aa. Both roc test runs pass, the game builds and runs, and alloc-check passes with 3 for entity-game.
